He spends 10 to 12 hours daily in front of computer screens and often forgets to take breaks. He reports that symptoms improve on weekends when he reduces screen time. He denies blurred vision, floaters, flashes of light, or eye pain. He does not wear corrective lenses. On examination, visual acuity is 20/20 bilaterally. Extraocular movements are intact. Pupils are equal and reactive. Conjunctivae are mildly injected. The anterior segment and fundoscopic exams are normal bilaterally.

A 56-year-old woman with a history of smoking presents to her primary care physician with shortness of breath and cough for several days. Her symptoms began 3 days ago with rhinorrhea. She reports a chronic morning cough productive of white sputum, which has increased over the past 2 days. She has had similar episodes each winter for the past 4 years. She has smoked 1 to 2 packs of cigarettes per day for 40 years and continues to smoke. She denies hemoptysis, chills, or weight loss and has not received any relief from over-the-counter cough preparations.

A 25-year-old woman presents with 3 days of clear nasal discharge, mild sore throat, and occasional sneezing. She works as a daycare teacher and reports several children in her class have had similar symptoms. She denies fever, cough, dyspnea, ear pain, or facial pressure. On examination, temperature is 37.0°C. The oropharynx shows mild erythema without exudates. Nasal mucosa is mildly edematous with clear discharge. Tympanic membranes are normal bilaterally. Cervical lymph nodes are not enlarged. She is well-appearing and in no distress.

A 5-year-old boy is brought in by his mother who noticed multiple itchy red bumps on his arms and legs after he spent the afternoon playing outside in the backyard. The bumps appeared over the past 24 hours. He has been scratching but the mother reports no significant swelling beyond the immediate area of each bump. He denies fever, joint pain, or any recent travel. On examination, there are approximately 8 to 10 small erythematous papules, each 3 to 5 mm in diameter, scattered on the bilateral forearms and lower legs. Several have small central puncta. There is no surrounding cellulitis, lymphangitis, or regional lymphadenopathy.

A 24-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of dysuria and urinary frequency that has progressed to right flank pain, fever, and rigors over the past 24 hours. She reports nausea and one episode of vomiting. She has had two previous urinary tract infections in the past year treated with antibiotics. She is sexually active and uses oral contraceptives. She denies vaginal discharge or hematuria. Vital signs show temperature 102.2°F, heart rate 104, blood pressure 108/66, respiratory rate 18. On examination, she appears flushed and mildly uncomfortable. There is significant right costovertebral angle tenderness on percussion. Abdominal exam reveals mild suprapubic tenderness without guarding. Urinalysis shows large leukocyte esterase, positive nitrites, many white blood cells, and bacteria. A point-of-care pregnancy test is negative.

A 77-year-old man reports a 5-day history of burning and aching pain on the right side of his chest. This is followed by the development of erythema and a maculopapular rash in this painful area, accompanied by headache and malaise. The rash progressed to develop clusters of clear vesicles for 3 to 5 days, evolving through stages of pustulation, ulceration, and crusting.

A 28-year-old woman with known epilepsy is brought in by ambulance after her roommate witnessed continuous generalized tonic-clonic seizure activity for approximately 12 minutes. EMS administered 10 mg of intramuscular midazolam en route, but seizure activity persisted. Her past medical history includes focal epilepsy diagnosed at age 16, treated with levetiracetam. Her roommate reports she recently missed several doses of medication due to insurance issues. On arrival, she remains in continuous generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Vital signs: T 39.2C, HR 142, RR (irregular, 8-30), BP 168/98, SpO2 88% on non-rebreather mask. She is cyanotic around the lips. Finger-stick glucose is 142 mg/dL. IV lorazepam 4 mg is administered with brief cessation of convulsive activity, but seizures resume within 2 minutes.

A 31-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 6-month history of nipple discharge. She
has noticed that her breasts are tender and both nipples produce milky discharge on applying
mild pressure. She has not noted any bloody or clear nipple discharge, breast lumps, or skin
changes. She also states she has not had a menstrual period for 6 months, and her periods had
been irregular for 8 months before they stopped altogether. Prior to her menstrual irregularities,
her menses occurred at a normal frequency and duration. She is sexually active with a single
partner and is trying to conceive.

A 44-year-old woman with known Addison disease on chronic hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone replacement presents with 3 days of progressive nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain following a viral gastroenteritis illness. She has been unable to keep her oral medications down for 2 days. On examination, she is lethargic and appears critically ill with notable hyperpigmentation of the oral mucosa, palmar creases, and surgical scars. Vital signs: T 37.8C, HR 118, RR 22, BP 72/38 (unresponsive to 2L IV normal saline), SpO2 95%. Skin turgor is markedly decreased. Labs: sodium 118 mEq/L, potassium 6.4 mEq/L, glucose 52 mg/dL, BUN 48 mg/dL, creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, random cortisol 1.2 mcg/dL. ECG shows peaked T waves and prolonged PR interval. IV stress-dose hydrocortisone 100 mg is administered immediately.

A 55-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 11.2%) presents with rapidly worsening pain, swelling, and redness of his right lower leg that began 2 days ago after a minor abrasion he sustained while gardening. Despite oral cephalexin started by his PCP yesterday, the erythema has expanded dramatically. On examination, he appears toxic and diaphoretic. Vital signs: T 39.8C, HR 128, RR 24, BP 92/56, SpO2 95%. The right leg demonstrates tense, dusky erythema extending from the ankle to the knee with areas of purplish discoloration and hemorrhagic bullae. Crepitus is palpable along the anterior shin. Pain is severe and extends beyond the visible margins of erythema. Labs: WBC 28,200/mcL, glucose 428 mg/dL, sodium 131 mEq/L, creatinine 2.4 mg/dL, CRP 32 mg/dL, lactate 4.6 mmol/L. LRINEC score is 10. CT of the leg shows extensive gas tracking along the fascial planes.

A 20-year-old male college athlete presents with itchy, peeling skin between his toes bilaterally for the past 2 weeks. He plays on the soccer team and uses communal showers at the athletic facility daily. He denies pain, swelling, or spreading beyond the interdigital spaces. He has no history of diabetes or immunosuppression. On examination, there is maceration and peeling of the skin in the third and fourth interdigital web spaces of both feet. Mild erythema is present. There are no vesicles, bullae, or fissures extending to the soles. Toenails appear normal.

A 14-year-old boy presents with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Eighteen hours earlier, he had been at a picnic where he ingested undercooked chicken along with a variety of other foods. He reports moderate-volume, nonbloody stools occurring 6 times a day. He has mild abdominal cramps and a low-grade fever. He is evaluated at an acute care clinic and found to be mildly tachycardic (heart rate 105 bpm) with a normal BP and a low-grade temperature of 100.1°F (37.8°C). His physical exam is unremarkable except for mild diffuse abdominal tenderness and mild increased bowel sounds. He is able to take oral fluids and is instructed on the appropriate oral fluid and electrolyte rehydration.

A 21-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 3-day history of
progressively worsening right scrotal pain. He says the pain started 3 days ago when he woke
up. At first, the pain was a minor annoyance, but it has gradually increased in intensity to the
point that it is now somewhat uncomfortable to walk. He has also noted a gradual swelling of his
right scrotum but denies penile discharge, urinary frequency, dysuria, hematuria, or fevers. He
denies any trauma to the area. He competed in a basketball game the previous evening but did
not feel as though he strained himself during the game. He denies experiencing anything like
this in the past. He has taken acetaminophen for the scrotal pain without any relief.

A 62-year-old woman with a history of osteoarthritis managed with daily naproxen for the past 3 years presents with a 4-week history of gnawing epigastric pain, early satiety, and occasional nausea. The pain is worse on an empty stomach and partially relieved by eating. She denies vomiting, hematemesis, melena, or unintentional weight loss. She does not smoke but drinks one glass of wine nightly. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination reveals mild epigastric tenderness on deep palpation without rebound or guarding. Bowel sounds are normoactive. There is no hepatosplenomegaly. A fecal occult blood test is negative. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin of 12.1 g/dL.

A 34-year-old man presents to urgent care after twisting his left ankle while stepping off a curb earlier today. He describes an inversion mechanism and reports hearing a crack at the time of injury. He is unable to bear weight on the left foot. He denies any previous ankle injuries. On examination, there is significant swelling and ecchymosis over the lateral malleolus. Point tenderness is present over the distal fibula with palpable bony tenderness at the posterior edge of the lateral malleolus. The medial malleolus is nontender. Anterior drawer test of the ankle is difficult to assess due to pain and guarding. Neurovascular status of the foot is intact with brisk capillary refill and intact sensation. Ankle radiographs demonstrate a non-displaced transverse fracture of the distal fibula (Weber B) with no talar shift.

A 40-year-old man presents with difficulty falling and staying asleep over the past 5 nights. He recently took on a major project at work with a tight deadline and reports feeling anxious about it. He estimates sleeping only 4 to 5 hours per night and experiencing daytime fatigue and difficulty concentrating. He denies depressed mood, loss of interest in activities, or suicidal ideation. He has no history of sleep disorders. He consumes coffee until mid-afternoon. On examination, he is well-groomed but appears mildly fatigued. Vital signs are normal. Neurological exam and mental status exam are unremarkable.

A 5-year-old girl is brought to the clinic by her parents for a spreading rash around her mouth and nose that began 5 days ago. It started as a small red spot near her left nostril and has since developed into multiple crusty lesions. Several children at her daycare have had similar sores. She is otherwise well with no fever, sore throat, or decreased appetite. On examination, there are multiple well-defined erosions with thick golden-yellow (honey-colored) crusts clustered around the nares and upper lip, with two satellite lesions on the left cheek. The lesions range from 1 to 3 cm in size. There is no warmth, fluctuance, or deep tissue involvement. There is mild left submandibular lymphadenopathy. The remainder of the skin examination is normal. She has no history of eczema or immunodeficiency.

A 47-yr-old woman comes to the office because of an 8-wk history of a cough. She says the
cough is never productive, occurs at all times of the day (including at night), and is independent
of activity. She is not sure whether she had an upper respiratory tract infection preceding the
cough. She does recall that a new neighbor, who is a smoker, moved into a downstairs
apartment at the time the cough began. The neighbor frequently smokes outside the patient's
apartment window, triggering the cough.
She has not noticed any heartburn or runny nose. One month after the cough started, she
noticed pain at the right side of her breastbone occurring with stretching and deep breathing. At
that same time, she also noted that she has been wheezing during exertion. She has never had
wheezing before. She has had no shortness of breath.

An 8-year-old girl is brought to the pediatrician by her mother for intense itching that has been worsening over the past 2 weeks. The itching is particularly severe at night and disrupts her sleep. Her mother reports that her younger brother and father have recently developed similar itching. On examination, there are numerous small erythematous papules and excoriations in the interdigital web spaces of both hands, the flexor surfaces of the wrists, the axillary folds, and the periumbilical area. Several short, linear burrows approximately 5 to 10 mm in length are visible in the web spaces between the fingers. The face and scalp are spared. There are no vesicles or bullae. A mineral oil preparation from a burrow scraping examined under microscopy reveals mites, eggs, and fecal pellets.

A 49-yr-old woman comes to the emergency department because of chest pain. She says she
was in her usual state of health until the day before, when she awoke at 6 am with the sudden
onset of sharp left-sided chest pain. Pain has been constant and radiates to the center of her
chest. It is not worsened by exertion, movement, food, activity, or respiration. She also had
shortness of breath and chills but no cough, nausea, or diaphoresis. She took 400 mg of
naproxen without relief. The pain has persisted, prompting her to come to the emergency
department now. She has never had chest pain before this episode and has no known history of
cardiac or pulmonary disease.

A 72-year-old man with a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia and recent urinary tract infection treated with oral antibiotics presents with 2 days of worsening confusion, fever, and decreased oral intake. His wife reports he has been increasingly lethargic and today was unable to recognize her. On examination, he is obtunded, with warm, flushed skin. Vital signs: T 39.4C, HR 122, RR 26, BP 76/44 (MAP 55), SpO2 93% on room air. Suprapubic tenderness is present with a distended bladder. Foley catheter insertion yields 800 mL of cloudy, foul-smelling urine. Labs: WBC 24,800/mcL with 22% bands, creatinine 3.2 mg/dL (baseline 1.2), lactate 5.8 mmol/L, procalcitonin 48 ng/mL, platelets 82,000/mcL. Urinalysis shows too numerous to count WBC and bacteria. SOFA score is 11. Blood and urine cultures are obtained, and broad-spectrum antibiotics and IV fluid resuscitation are initiated.

A 38-year-old man is brought in by ambulance after sudden onset of severe vertigo, diplopia, and difficulty swallowing while at work 90 minutes ago. He has no significant past medical history and takes no medications. On examination, he is alert but dysarthric. Vital signs: T 37.0C, HR 78, RR 16, BP 168/94, SpO2 98%. Neurological exam reveals left-sided Horner syndrome, right-sided limb ataxia, decreased pain and temperature sensation on the left face and right body, and absent gag reflex on the left. CT head is negative for hemorrhage. CT angiography reveals left vertebral artery occlusion. NIHSS score is 12.

A 68-year-old man with a recent diagnosis of mild heart failure comes to the office because of a
1-week history of dyspnea on exertion. He is relatively sedentary but is usually able to climb a
flight of stairs without stopping. Now he must stop every few steps to rest because of dyspnea
but not chest discomfort. He also complains of lower extremity edema, 2-pillow orthopnea,
cough with occasional production of white phlegm, wheezing, and a 3-kg weight gain. He denies
chest pain or discomfort, palpitations, syncope or near syncope. He has had no fever or upper
respiratory symptoms. He states he has been compliant with his medications and denies any
changes to his diet. He was seen by another physician two times in the past few months for
similar symptoms; both times he had an ECG and chest x-ray and was told he had "mild heart
failure." He was treated with an increased dose of furosemide without any other workup.

A 50-year-old obese man with a BMI of 34 presents with a 6-month history of persistent heartburn and acid regurgitation despite taking omeprazole 20 mg daily. He reports the heartburn is worse after large meals and when lying down, and he frequently wakes at night with a sour taste in his mouth and occasional coughing. He has tried elevating the head of his bed and avoiding late meals with only partial relief. He denies dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, or hematemesis. He drinks two to three beers on weekends and does not smoke. On examination, vital signs are normal. He is an obese man in no acute distress. Abdominal exam reveals mild epigastric tenderness. There is no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. His dentist has noted enamel erosion on posterior teeth.

A 28-year-old woman presents with pain on the index finger of her left hand after accidentally touching a hot pan while cooking approximately 1 hour ago. She ran the finger under cool water immediately. She denies blistering, numbness, or limited range of motion. On examination, there is diffuse erythema of the palmar surface of the left index finger from the fingertip to the proximal interphalangeal joint. The skin is intact with no blistering or blanching. The area is tender to light touch and warm. Capillary refill is less than 2 seconds. Sensation and range of motion of the finger are intact.

A 20-year-old female college student presents with bilateral itchy, watery eyes for the past 3 days. She reports that the symptoms began shortly after spring pollen counts increased. She has a known history of seasonal allergies but has not yet started any medications this year. She denies eye pain, photophobia, purulent discharge, or changes in vision. On examination, bilateral conjunctival injection is noted with mild chemosis. There is clear watery discharge. Pupils are equal and reactive. Visual acuity is intact bilaterally. There is no preauricular lymphadenopathy.

A 26-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 3-day history of lower abdominal pain. She is 18 weeks pregnant by dates. The patient describes the pain as sharp, steady, and radiating across her lower abdomen bilaterally. Last night she developed new nausea and vomiting. She has not been able to keep down any food or drink this morning. She had a normal bowel movement yesterday. She says she felt cold and shivering this morning, followed by feeling warm; however, she did not check her temperature. She denies vaginal bleeding.

A 10-year-old girl is brought in by her parents who report she frequently feels nauseated and dizzy during car rides, particularly on winding roads. Symptoms have been occurring for the past year and typically resolve within 15 to 20 minutes after stopping the vehicle. She does not vomit. Sitting in the front seat and looking out the window helps somewhat. She denies hearing loss, tinnitus, headaches, or similar symptoms outside of car rides. On examination, she is well-appearing and in no distress. Vital signs are age-appropriate. Neurological exam, including cranial nerves and cerebellar testing, is normal. Otoscopic exam is unremarkable.

A 50-year-old man presents with intermittent burning sensation in the substernal area that he has experienced occasionally over the past several weeks. The burning typically occurs 30 to 60 minutes after large meals, particularly those that are spicy or high in fat. The discomfort is relieved within minutes by over-the-counter antacids. He denies dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, hematemesis, or melena. He has no cardiac history. On examination, vital signs are normal. The abdomen is soft, non-tender, and non-distended. There is no epigastric tenderness. Cardiac exam is unremarkable.

A 60-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of progressively worsening left lower quadrant abdominal pain that is constant and dull. She reports low-grade fever and mild nausea but no vomiting. She had a colonoscopy 2 years ago that showed extensive diverticulosis of the sigmoid colon. Her diet is low in fiber. She reports one episode of constipation followed by loose stools. Vital signs show temperature 100.8°F, heart rate 86, blood pressure 128/76. On examination, there is moderate tenderness in the left lower quadrant with voluntary guarding but no rebound tenderness or rigidity. Bowel sounds are present and hypoactive. There is no palpable mass. Laboratory work shows a white blood cell count of 13,200 with a left shift. CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast demonstrates sigmoid diverticulitis with pericolic fat stranding and no abscess or perforation.

A 12-year-old boy is brought to the office by his mother for a well-child checkup. The patient and his mother both state that the patient has been otherwise well except for occasional mild pain and stiffness in the upper back. Symptoms began gradually about a year ago and are present intermittently. The pain and stiffness do not bother him significantly or limit his activities, and they have never awakened him from sleep. He denies any trauma or overuse. He is not currently playing any organized sports although he is able to be normally active with friends and siblings.

A 19-year-old female college student is brought in by her roommate with a 24-hour history of high fever, diffuse rash, vomiting, profuse watery diarrhea, and progressive lightheadedness. She reports using a menstrual tampon that she forgot to change for approximately 3 days. On examination, she appears acutely ill with a diffuse, blanching, erythematous macular rash resembling a sunburn covering the trunk and extremities, including the palms and soles. Vital signs: T 40.2C, HR 136, RR 26, BP 72/40, SpO2 94%. Mucous membranes are hyperemic. Pelvic exam reveals a retained tampon, which is removed, and there is no evidence of abscess. Labs: WBC 15,400/mcL, platelets 88,000/mcL, creatinine 2.8 mg/dL, AST 245 U/L, ALT 198 U/L, CK 1,240 U/L. Blood cultures are drawn and empiric clindamycin and vancomycin are initiated.

A 32-year-old male singer presents with a hoarse voice that has persisted for 3 days following an intense concert performance. He reports mild sore throat and throat dryness but denies dyspnea, stridor, dysphagia, fever, or hemoptysis. He is a non-smoker and does not consume alcohol regularly. He has no history of GERD or thyroid disease. On examination, he is afebrile. The oropharynx is mildly erythematous without exudates or lesions. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy. His voice is notably hoarse and breathy. Respiratory effort is normal with no stridor or wheezing on auscultation.

A 6-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents after 8 hours of progressive wheezing and respiratory distress despite using his albuterol inhaler every 20 minutes at home. He has a history of moderate persistent asthma with two prior ICU admissions. He recently had an upper respiratory infection. On examination, he is sitting upright, using accessory muscles, and speaking in single words only. Vital signs: T 37.8C, HR 152, RR 42, BP 100/65, SpO2 87% on room air. Lung auscultation reveals markedly diminished breath sounds bilaterally with minimal wheezing, suggesting severe air trapping. Peak flow is unobtainable due to patient fatigue. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.28, pCO2 55 mmHg.

A 53-yr-old woman comes to the office because of palpitations. She is a current patient there
and has a history of well-controlled hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and tension headaches. She
states that she has noticed intermittent palpitations over the past 2 mo. She describes the
episodes as a sensation of irregular and racing heartbeats that are accompanied by fatigue.
She denies any chest pain, shortness of breath, light-headedness, or syncope. The episodes
last from 10 min to several hours, occur once or twice/wk, and resolve on their own. The last
episode was 3 days ago. She cannot identify any particular triggers. She is generally active and
walks 3 miles several days/wk without any exertional symptoms including chest pain and
dyspnea. She has no family history of early cardiac disease or sudden death. She denies any
recent fever or infectious symptoms.

A 72-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history and known COPD (GOLD stage II) presents with a 5-day history of increased sputum production and mild worsening of his baseline dyspnea. He reports his sputum has changed from white to yellow-green. He denies fever, chest pain, hemoptysis, or significant increase in cough frequency. He is currently using tiotropium and an albuterol rescue inhaler as needed. Vital signs show temperature 98.6°F, heart rate 82, blood pressure 134/78, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 93% on room air (baseline 94-95%). On examination, there is mild bilateral expiratory wheezing without accessory muscle use. He is speaking in full sentences comfortably.

A 72-year-old woman presents with generalized dry, itchy skin that has been worsening over the past several weeks as winter has progressed. She reports the itching is worst on her shins and forearms. She bathes daily in hot water and uses regular bar soap. She denies any new medications, rash, jaundice, or unintentional weight loss. On examination, the skin on the extremities is diffusely dry with fine scaling and superficial cracking. There are no excoriations, erythematous plaques, or papules. Skin turgor is appropriate for age. No jaundice or lymphadenopathy is noted.

A 20-year-old female college student who recently started a running program presents with bilateral dull, aching pain along the front of both shins. The pain began about 1 week ago and occurs primarily during and shortly after running, then resolves with rest. She runs on paved surfaces in her current athletic shoes that are over a year old. She denies pain at rest, nighttime pain, swelling, or history of stress fractures. On examination, there is mild tenderness on palpation along the medial border of the bilateral tibias spanning approximately 5 cm. There is no point tenderness, edema, or erythema. Ankle range of motion and strength are normal.

A 17-year-old female is brought in by her parents after they discovered an empty bottle of extra-strength acetaminophen (500 mg tablets, 50-count) in her room. She admits to intentionally ingesting approximately 25 grams 12 hours ago following a breakup. She initially felt fine but now reports nausea, vomiting, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. On examination, she is tearful but cooperative. Vital signs: T 37.2C, HR 96, RR 18, BP 112/68, SpO2 99%. Abdomen is tender in the right upper quadrant. Scleral icterus is not yet present. Labs: acetaminophen level 180 mcg/mL (well above treatment line on Rumack-Matthew nomogram at 12 hours), AST 1,240 U/L, ALT 1,086 U/L, INR 1.8, total bilirubin 2.1 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, pH 7.34, lactate 2.8 mmol/L. N-acetylcysteine infusion is initiated immediately. Psychiatry and social work consultations are placed. Poison control is contacted.

A 70-year-old man presents with 18 hours of worsening right upper quadrant pain, fever with rigors, and progressive yellowing of his skin and eyes. He has a history of choledocholithiasis with a prior ERCP and sphincterotomy 5 years ago. On examination, he appears jaundiced and acutely ill with intermittent rigors. Vital signs: T 39.6C, HR 118, RR 22, BP 88/52, SpO2 96%. Abdominal examination reveals significant right upper quadrant tenderness with a positive Murphy sign. Scleral icterus is prominent. Labs: WBC 22,600/mcL with 15% bands, total bilirubin 8.4 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 6.8 mg/dL, ALP 482 U/L, AST 188 U/L, ALT 162 U/L, lipase normal, lactate 4.1 mmol/L. Blood cultures are drawn. Right upper quadrant ultrasound shows common bile duct dilation to 14 mm with a shadowing stone in the distal CBD and mild intrahepatic ductal dilation.

A 3-year-old girl is brought in by her mother with a low-grade fever of 37.8°C and small blisters noticed on her hands and feet since this morning. The mother also notes a few small sores inside the child's mouth. The child is eating and drinking well, though slightly fussier than usual. Several children at her daycare have had similar symptoms. On examination, there are scattered small vesicles on the palms, soles, and a few on the dorsal hands. Two shallow ulcers are seen on the buccal mucosa. The child is alert, playful, and well-hydrated.

A 68-yr-old woman comes to the office with her daughter because of a 4-mo history of gradually
increasing lethargy and worsening memory. Her daughter is concerned because the mother has
stopped remembering whether she has taken her regular medications. The daughter is worried
that her mother might not be safe to live on her own. Prior to 4 mo ago, the woman had been
very busy with community activities, which she has since stopped, and her daughter had not
noticed any memory difficulties. The daughter is not aware of any recent illnesses or injuries.

Mrs. L is a 61 year-old woman who presents with 4 days of a cough productive of yellow sputum. Her symptoms started 4 days ago with rhinorrhea and productive cough. She initially had fevers as high as 101 for 2 days, but those have now resolved. In the office, she has normal vital signs and a normal physical examination. She is otherwise healthy except for high cholesterol for which she is being treated with atorvastatin. She has no drug allergies.

A 9-month-old male infant is brought in by his parents after 8 hours of episodic inconsolable crying during which he draws his legs up to his abdomen, alternating with periods of lethargy. The parents report two episodes of vomiting and one bowel movement containing dark red mucus-like material. He had a viral upper respiratory infection last week. On examination, during a pain-free interval, the infant is pale and lethargic. Vital signs: T 37.4C, HR 168, RR 36, BP 80/52. Abdomen is mildly distended with a palpable sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant. The right lower quadrant feels empty (Dance sign). Rectal exam reveals currant jelly stool on the examining finger. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates a target sign (doughnut sign) in the right upper quadrant, confirming ileocolic intussusception, with no evidence of perforation or peritonitis. Air enema reduction is arranged.

A 70-year-old man with a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia presents to his primary care physician with a 3-day history of dysuria, urinary frequency, and urgency. He reports mild suprapubic discomfort and low-grade fever of 100.4°F. He denies flank pain, rigors, or hematuria. His past medical history is notable for BPH managed with tamsulosin. On examination, he appears mildly uncomfortable but is in no acute distress. Vital signs show temperature 100.4°F, blood pressure 138/82, heart rate 78. Abdominal examination reveals mild suprapubic tenderness without guarding. Digital rectal exam shows an enlarged, nontender prostate. Urinalysis demonstrates pyuria and positive nitrites.

A 66-year-old woman presents with 2 days of progressive abdominal distension, diffuse crampy abdominal pain, and intractable vomiting that has become bilious and feculent. She has not passed flatus or had a bowel movement for 36 hours. Her surgical history includes an open appendectomy 30 years ago and a total abdominal hysterectomy 15 years ago. On examination, she appears dehydrated and in moderate distress. Vital signs: T 37.8C, HR 110, RR 20, BP 108/68, SpO2 97%. Abdomen is markedly distended and tympanitic with high-pitched tinkling bowel sounds. There is diffuse tenderness, greatest in the periumbilical region, with mild involuntary guarding. Labs: WBC 14,800/mcL, BUN 42, creatinine 1.6, lactate 3.1 mmol/L. CT abdomen demonstrates dilated small bowel loops up to 5.2 cm with a discrete transition point in the right lower quadrant with a small bowel feces sign and possible closed-loop configuration.

A 40-year-old male construction worker is extricated by rescue crews after being trapped under a collapsed concrete wall at a building site for approximately 4 hours. Both lower extremities were pinned. Upon extrication, he is alert and reports severe pain in both legs and a sensation of numbness. He has no significant past medical history. On examination, both lower extremities are markedly swollen, tense, and ecchymotic from the thighs to the ankles. Vital signs: T 36.4C, HR 118, RR 24, BP 96/62, SpO2 95%. Pedal pulses are weak bilaterally. Sensation is diminished throughout both legs. He reports dark brown urine since a Foley catheter was placed in the field, with only 50 mL output over the past 2 hours. Labs drawn immediately: potassium 6.8 mEq/L, creatinine 3.4 mg/dL, CK 124,000 U/L, phosphorus 7.6 mg/dL, calcium 6.2 mg/dL, uric acid 14.2 mg/dL, myoglobin 48,000 ng/mL, bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, lactate 6.8 mmol/L. ECG shows peaked T waves. Aggressive IV normal saline resuscitation at 1.5 L/hr with sodium bicarbonate supplementation is initiated, along with continuous cardiac monitoring and IV calcium gluconate for cardioprotection.

A 47-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of the worst headache of her life that began 1 hour ago while straining during a bowel movement. She describes it as a thunderclap headache reaching maximum intensity within seconds. She experienced one episode of vomiting and brief loss of consciousness. Her past medical history includes migraines and she is a current smoker. On examination, she is photophobic, irritable, and has a stiff neck. Vital signs: T 37.4C, HR 96, RR 18, BP 178/96, SpO2 98%. Neurological exam reveals intact cranial nerves, mild bilateral lower extremity weakness, and pronounced nuchal rigidity. Hunt and Hess grade III. Non-contrast CT head reveals diffuse subarachnoid hemorrhage in the basal cisterns. CT angiography identifies a 7 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm.

A 5-month-old baby boy presents with difficulty and delay in passing hard stools. His mother reports that he strains for several hours and may even miss a day, before passing stool with screaming and occasional spots of fresh blood on the stool or diaper. He has recently been weaned from breastfeeding to cows' milk formula, which he had been reluctant to drink initially. The child is thriving and now feeding normally. There was no neonatal delay in defecation and no history of excessive vomiting or abdominal distension.

A 65-year-old man presents to the emergency department with acute onset of SOB of 30 minutes' duration. Initially, he felt faint but did not lose consciousness. He is complaining of left-sided chest pain that worsens on deep inspiration. He has no history of cardiopulmonary disease. A week ago he underwent a total left hip replacement and, following discharge, was on bed rest for 3 days due to poorly controlled pain. He subsequently noticed swelling in his left calf, which is tender on examination. His current vital signs reveal a fever of 100.4°F (38.0°C), heart rate 112 bpm, BP 95/65, and an O2 saturation on room air of 91%.

A 32-year-old woman at 34 weeks gestation (G3P2) presents with sudden onset of painful vaginal bleeding and severe constant abdominal pain that began 30 minutes ago. She has a history of chronic hypertension managed with labetalol and a prior placental abruption with her second pregnancy. She reports the baby's movements have decreased since the bleeding started. On examination, she is anxious, pale, and in significant distress. Vital signs: T 36.8C, HR 124, RR 24, BP 96/62, SpO2 96%. The uterus is firm, tender, and contracted (woody consistency) with no relaxation between contractions. Moderate dark red vaginal bleeding is present. Continuous fetal monitoring reveals a baseline fetal heart rate of 170 bpm with absent variability and repetitive late decelerations. Labs: hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL, platelets 108,000/mcL, fibrinogen 142 mg/dL (low), PT 14.8 seconds, D-dimer >20,000 ng/mL. Transfusion is initiated and emergent cesarean delivery is called.

A 30-year-old man presents to the urgent care clinic with a 6-hour history of severe pain, tearing, and foreign body sensation in his left eye. He was grinding metal at work without wearing safety goggles when he felt something strike his eye. Since then, he has had constant sharp pain, profuse tearing, photophobia, and difficulty keeping the eye open. He denies any change in vision other than blurriness from tearing. He wears contact lenses but removed them immediately after the incident. On examination, visual acuity is 20/30 in the left eye (baseline 20/20) and 20/20 in the right. There is conjunctival injection of the left eye with no hypopyon or hyphema. The pupil is round and reactive. Fluorescein staining under cobalt blue light reveals a 3 mm linear epithelial defect on the central cornea. Seidel test is negative. There is no retained foreign body visible on slit lamp examination or eversion of the upper lid.

A 68-year-old man presents with sudden onset of severe pain, coldness, and numbness in his left leg that started approximately 3 hours ago while sitting at home. He has a history of atrial fibrillation and was recently taken off warfarin due to a GI bleed. On examination, the left leg is pale and cool to the touch from the mid-thigh distally. Vital signs: T 36.9C, HR 88 (irregularly irregular), RR 16, BP 148/86, SpO2 97%. Left dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are absent by palpation and Doppler. Left popliteal pulse is faintly detectable. The left calf is tender with decreased sensation and the patient is unable to dorsiflex or plantarflex the left foot. Right leg pulses are palpable and symmetric. CT angiography shows abrupt occlusion of the left superficial femoral artery.

An 8-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after pulling a pot of boiling water off the stove onto himself approximately 45 minutes ago. He sustained scald burns to his anterior chest, abdomen, both upper extremities, and portions of his face. He has been crying inconsolably. He has no significant past medical history. On examination, he is alert but in severe pain and distress. Vital signs: T 36.6C, HR 152, RR 28, BP 94/58, SpO2 98%. Weight is 28 kg. Burns cover approximately 20% total body surface area: areas of erythema with large intact and ruptured blisters (superficial partial thickness) on the chest and abdomen, with waxy white insensate areas (deep partial to full thickness) on both forearms. No circumferential burns are identified. Facial burns are superficial with no singed nasal hairs and no evidence of inhalation injury. He has no hoarseness or stridor. Parkland formula is calculated (20% TBSA x 28 kg x 4 mL = 2,240 mL LR over first 24 hours), IV access is obtained, and morphine is administered for pain.

A 29-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician reporting 8 months of near-constant excessive worry about multiple domains of her life including work performance, finances, health, and her children's safety. She describes an inability to control the worry despite recognizing it is disproportionate. She reports associated restlessness, muscle tension predominantly in her neck and shoulders, difficulty falling asleep, irritability, and difficulty concentrating during meetings. She has tried meditation and exercise with only partial benefit. She denies panic attacks, specific phobias, obsessive thoughts, or traumatic experiences. She has no prior psychiatric history and takes no medications. She drinks one cup of coffee daily. Vital signs are normal. Physical examination reveals bilateral trapezius muscle tightness but is otherwise unremarkable. Thyroid function tests are within normal limits. GAD-7 score is 16 indicating severe anxiety.

A 40-year-old woman presents with a 2-year history of persistent nasal congestion, frequent sneezing, and clear rhinorrhea. She notes that symptoms are present year-round but worsen when she vacuums or dusts her home. She denies any history of asthma, wheezing, or shortness of breath. She has tried over-the-counter antihistamines intermittently with partial relief. On examination, nasal mucosa is pale and boggy bilaterally. There is a transverse nasal crease. No nasal polyps are visualized. Lungs are clear to auscultation. She lives in an older home with carpeted bedrooms and reports no pets.

A 16-year-old female high school student presents with complaints of fever, sore throat, and fatigue. She started feeling sick 1 week ago. Her symptoms are gradually getting worse, and she has difficulty swallowing. She has had a fever every day, and she could hardly get out of bed this morning. She does not remember being exposed to anybody with a similar illness recently. On physical examination she is febrile and looks sick. Enlarged cervical lymph nodes, exudative pharyngitis with soft palate petechiae and faint erythematous macular rash on the trunk and arms are found.

A 4-year-old boy is brought in by his parents after 6 hours of rapidly progressive sore throat, difficulty swallowing, and noisy breathing. He has had no significant past medical history and immunizations are not up to date (parents declined some vaccines). On examination, the child is sitting upright in a tripod position, leaning forward with his neck extended and jaw thrust forward. He is drooling profusely and appears anxious and toxic-appearing. Vital signs: T 39.8C, HR 162, RR 34, SpO2 92% on room air. Inspiratory stridor is audible without a stethoscope. His voice is muffled and he refuses to speak or drink. A soft tissue lateral neck X-ray obtained reveals a thumb sign consistent with epiglottic swelling. Anesthesiology and ENT are urgently called for airway management.

A 35-year-old man is referred by his primary care physician for psychiatric evaluation after presenting with a 2-month history of persistent low mood, loss of interest in activities he previously enjoyed including playing guitar and socializing, insomnia with early morning awakening, decreased appetite with an unintentional 14-pound weight loss, difficulty concentrating at work, and pervasive feelings of worthlessness. He describes his mood as an overwhelming heaviness that does not lift. He has been increasingly isolating from friends and family. He denies suicidal ideation, hallucinations, or delusions. He has no prior psychiatric history. He went through a significant relationship breakup 3 months ago. Vital signs are normal. On mental status examination, he is casually dressed with poor grooming. Psychomotor retardation is present. Speech is soft and slow. Affect is flat. Thought process is linear but impoverished. PHQ-9 score is 22 indicating severe depression.

A 72-year-old man presents with 3 days of vague periumbilical discomfort that has gradually localized to the right lower quadrant. He reports decreased appetite, mild nausea, and one episode of loose stool. His past medical history includes type 2 diabetes, coronary artery disease, and a total knee replacement. On examination, he is afebrile at 37.2C but appears mildly uncomfortable. Vital signs: HR 92, RR 18, BP 134/78, SpO2 97%. Abdominal exam reveals mild right lower quadrant tenderness without guarding or rebound. WBC is only mildly elevated at 11,200/mcL. CT abdomen with contrast shows a dilated appendix measuring 14 mm with periappendiceal fat stranding and a small contained fluid collection suggestive of early perforation.

A 29-year-old male software developer presents with eye fatigue, dryness, and a mild headache that worsens throughout the workday. He spends 10 to 12 hours daily in front of computer screens and often forgets to take breaks. He reports that symptoms improve on weekends when he reduces screen time. He denies blurred vision, floaters, flashes of light, or eye pain. He does not wear corrective lenses. On examination, visual acuity is 20/20 bilaterally. Extraocular movements are intact. Pupils are equal and reactive. Conjunctivae are mildly injected. The anterior segment and fundoscopic exams are normal bilaterally.

A 56-year-old woman with a history of smoking presents to her primary care physician with shortness of breath and cough for several days. Her symptoms began 3 days ago with rhinorrhea. She reports a chronic morning cough productive of white sputum, which has increased over the past 2 days. She has had similar episodes each winter for the past 4 years. She has smoked 1 to 2 packs of cigarettes per day for 40 years and continues to smoke. She denies hemoptysis, chills, or weight loss and has not received any relief from over-the-counter cough preparations.

A 25-year-old woman presents with 3 days of clear nasal discharge, mild sore throat, and occasional sneezing. She works as a daycare teacher and reports several children in her class have had similar symptoms. She denies fever, cough, dyspnea, ear pain, or facial pressure. On examination, temperature is 37.0°C. The oropharynx shows mild erythema without exudates. Nasal mucosa is mildly edematous with clear discharge. Tympanic membranes are normal bilaterally. Cervical lymph nodes are not enlarged. She is well-appearing and in no distress.

A 5-year-old boy is brought in by his mother who noticed multiple itchy red bumps on his arms and legs after he spent the afternoon playing outside in the backyard. The bumps appeared over the past 24 hours. He has been scratching but the mother reports no significant swelling beyond the immediate area of each bump. He denies fever, joint pain, or any recent travel. On examination, there are approximately 8 to 10 small erythematous papules, each 3 to 5 mm in diameter, scattered on the bilateral forearms and lower legs. Several have small central puncta. There is no surrounding cellulitis, lymphangitis, or regional lymphadenopathy.

A 24-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of dysuria and urinary frequency that has progressed to right flank pain, fever, and rigors over the past 24 hours. She reports nausea and one episode of vomiting. She has had two previous urinary tract infections in the past year treated with antibiotics. She is sexually active and uses oral contraceptives. She denies vaginal discharge or hematuria. Vital signs show temperature 102.2°F, heart rate 104, blood pressure 108/66, respiratory rate 18. On examination, she appears flushed and mildly uncomfortable. There is significant right costovertebral angle tenderness on percussion. Abdominal exam reveals mild suprapubic tenderness without guarding. Urinalysis shows large leukocyte esterase, positive nitrites, many white blood cells, and bacteria. A point-of-care pregnancy test is negative.

A 77-year-old man reports a 5-day history of burning and aching pain on the right side of his chest. This is followed by the development of erythema and a maculopapular rash in this painful area, accompanied by headache and malaise. The rash progressed to develop clusters of clear vesicles for 3 to 5 days, evolving through stages of pustulation, ulceration, and crusting.

A 28-year-old woman with known epilepsy is brought in by ambulance after her roommate witnessed continuous generalized tonic-clonic seizure activity for approximately 12 minutes. EMS administered 10 mg of intramuscular midazolam en route, but seizure activity persisted. Her past medical history includes focal epilepsy diagnosed at age 16, treated with levetiracetam. Her roommate reports she recently missed several doses of medication due to insurance issues. On arrival, she remains in continuous generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Vital signs: T 39.2C, HR 142, RR (irregular, 8-30), BP 168/98, SpO2 88% on non-rebreather mask. She is cyanotic around the lips. Finger-stick glucose is 142 mg/dL. IV lorazepam 4 mg is administered with brief cessation of convulsive activity, but seizures resume within 2 minutes.

A 31-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 6-month history of nipple discharge. She
has noticed that her breasts are tender and both nipples produce milky discharge on applying
mild pressure. She has not noted any bloody or clear nipple discharge, breast lumps, or skin
changes. She also states she has not had a menstrual period for 6 months, and her periods had
been irregular for 8 months before they stopped altogether. Prior to her menstrual irregularities,
her menses occurred at a normal frequency and duration. She is sexually active with a single
partner and is trying to conceive.

A 44-year-old woman with known Addison disease on chronic hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone replacement presents with 3 days of progressive nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain following a viral gastroenteritis illness. She has been unable to keep her oral medications down for 2 days. On examination, she is lethargic and appears critically ill with notable hyperpigmentation of the oral mucosa, palmar creases, and surgical scars. Vital signs: T 37.8C, HR 118, RR 22, BP 72/38 (unresponsive to 2L IV normal saline), SpO2 95%. Skin turgor is markedly decreased. Labs: sodium 118 mEq/L, potassium 6.4 mEq/L, glucose 52 mg/dL, BUN 48 mg/dL, creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, random cortisol 1.2 mcg/dL. ECG shows peaked T waves and prolonged PR interval. IV stress-dose hydrocortisone 100 mg is administered immediately.

A 55-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 11.2%) presents with rapidly worsening pain, swelling, and redness of his right lower leg that began 2 days ago after a minor abrasion he sustained while gardening. Despite oral cephalexin started by his PCP yesterday, the erythema has expanded dramatically. On examination, he appears toxic and diaphoretic. Vital signs: T 39.8C, HR 128, RR 24, BP 92/56, SpO2 95%. The right leg demonstrates tense, dusky erythema extending from the ankle to the knee with areas of purplish discoloration and hemorrhagic bullae. Crepitus is palpable along the anterior shin. Pain is severe and extends beyond the visible margins of erythema. Labs: WBC 28,200/mcL, glucose 428 mg/dL, sodium 131 mEq/L, creatinine 2.4 mg/dL, CRP 32 mg/dL, lactate 4.6 mmol/L. LRINEC score is 10. CT of the leg shows extensive gas tracking along the fascial planes.

A 20-year-old male college athlete presents with itchy, peeling skin between his toes bilaterally for the past 2 weeks. He plays on the soccer team and uses communal showers at the athletic facility daily. He denies pain, swelling, or spreading beyond the interdigital spaces. He has no history of diabetes or immunosuppression. On examination, there is maceration and peeling of the skin in the third and fourth interdigital web spaces of both feet. Mild erythema is present. There are no vesicles, bullae, or fissures extending to the soles. Toenails appear normal.

A 14-year-old boy presents with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Eighteen hours earlier, he had been at a picnic where he ingested undercooked chicken along with a variety of other foods. He reports moderate-volume, nonbloody stools occurring 6 times a day. He has mild abdominal cramps and a low-grade fever. He is evaluated at an acute care clinic and found to be mildly tachycardic (heart rate 105 bpm) with a normal BP and a low-grade temperature of 100.1°F (37.8°C). His physical exam is unremarkable except for mild diffuse abdominal tenderness and mild increased bowel sounds. He is able to take oral fluids and is instructed on the appropriate oral fluid and electrolyte rehydration.

A 21-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 3-day history of
progressively worsening right scrotal pain. He says the pain started 3 days ago when he woke
up. At first, the pain was a minor annoyance, but it has gradually increased in intensity to the
point that it is now somewhat uncomfortable to walk. He has also noted a gradual swelling of his
right scrotum but denies penile discharge, urinary frequency, dysuria, hematuria, or fevers. He
denies any trauma to the area. He competed in a basketball game the previous evening but did
not feel as though he strained himself during the game. He denies experiencing anything like
this in the past. He has taken acetaminophen for the scrotal pain without any relief.

A 62-year-old woman with a history of osteoarthritis managed with daily naproxen for the past 3 years presents with a 4-week history of gnawing epigastric pain, early satiety, and occasional nausea. The pain is worse on an empty stomach and partially relieved by eating. She denies vomiting, hematemesis, melena, or unintentional weight loss. She does not smoke but drinks one glass of wine nightly. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination reveals mild epigastric tenderness on deep palpation without rebound or guarding. Bowel sounds are normoactive. There is no hepatosplenomegaly. A fecal occult blood test is negative. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin of 12.1 g/dL.

A 34-year-old man presents to urgent care after twisting his left ankle while stepping off a curb earlier today. He describes an inversion mechanism and reports hearing a crack at the time of injury. He is unable to bear weight on the left foot. He denies any previous ankle injuries. On examination, there is significant swelling and ecchymosis over the lateral malleolus. Point tenderness is present over the distal fibula with palpable bony tenderness at the posterior edge of the lateral malleolus. The medial malleolus is nontender. Anterior drawer test of the ankle is difficult to assess due to pain and guarding. Neurovascular status of the foot is intact with brisk capillary refill and intact sensation. Ankle radiographs demonstrate a non-displaced transverse fracture of the distal fibula (Weber B) with no talar shift.

A 40-year-old man presents with difficulty falling and staying asleep over the past 5 nights. He recently took on a major project at work with a tight deadline and reports feeling anxious about it. He estimates sleeping only 4 to 5 hours per night and experiencing daytime fatigue and difficulty concentrating. He denies depressed mood, loss of interest in activities, or suicidal ideation. He has no history of sleep disorders. He consumes coffee until mid-afternoon. On examination, he is well-groomed but appears mildly fatigued. Vital signs are normal. Neurological exam and mental status exam are unremarkable.

A 5-year-old girl is brought to the clinic by her parents for a spreading rash around her mouth and nose that began 5 days ago. It started as a small red spot near her left nostril and has since developed into multiple crusty lesions. Several children at her daycare have had similar sores. She is otherwise well with no fever, sore throat, or decreased appetite. On examination, there are multiple well-defined erosions with thick golden-yellow (honey-colored) crusts clustered around the nares and upper lip, with two satellite lesions on the left cheek. The lesions range from 1 to 3 cm in size. There is no warmth, fluctuance, or deep tissue involvement. There is mild left submandibular lymphadenopathy. The remainder of the skin examination is normal. She has no history of eczema or immunodeficiency.

A 47-yr-old woman comes to the office because of an 8-wk history of a cough. She says the
cough is never productive, occurs at all times of the day (including at night), and is independent
of activity. She is not sure whether she had an upper respiratory tract infection preceding the
cough. She does recall that a new neighbor, who is a smoker, moved into a downstairs
apartment at the time the cough began. The neighbor frequently smokes outside the patient's
apartment window, triggering the cough.
She has not noticed any heartburn or runny nose. One month after the cough started, she
noticed pain at the right side of her breastbone occurring with stretching and deep breathing. At
that same time, she also noted that she has been wheezing during exertion. She has never had
wheezing before. She has had no shortness of breath.

An 8-year-old girl is brought to the pediatrician by her mother for intense itching that has been worsening over the past 2 weeks. The itching is particularly severe at night and disrupts her sleep. Her mother reports that her younger brother and father have recently developed similar itching. On examination, there are numerous small erythematous papules and excoriations in the interdigital web spaces of both hands, the flexor surfaces of the wrists, the axillary folds, and the periumbilical area. Several short, linear burrows approximately 5 to 10 mm in length are visible in the web spaces between the fingers. The face and scalp are spared. There are no vesicles or bullae. A mineral oil preparation from a burrow scraping examined under microscopy reveals mites, eggs, and fecal pellets.

A 49-yr-old woman comes to the emergency department because of chest pain. She says she
was in her usual state of health until the day before, when she awoke at 6 am with the sudden
onset of sharp left-sided chest pain. Pain has been constant and radiates to the center of her
chest. It is not worsened by exertion, movement, food, activity, or respiration. She also had
shortness of breath and chills but no cough, nausea, or diaphoresis. She took 400 mg of
naproxen without relief. The pain has persisted, prompting her to come to the emergency
department now. She has never had chest pain before this episode and has no known history of
cardiac or pulmonary disease.

A 72-year-old man with a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia and recent urinary tract infection treated with oral antibiotics presents with 2 days of worsening confusion, fever, and decreased oral intake. His wife reports he has been increasingly lethargic and today was unable to recognize her. On examination, he is obtunded, with warm, flushed skin. Vital signs: T 39.4C, HR 122, RR 26, BP 76/44 (MAP 55), SpO2 93% on room air. Suprapubic tenderness is present with a distended bladder. Foley catheter insertion yields 800 mL of cloudy, foul-smelling urine. Labs: WBC 24,800/mcL with 22% bands, creatinine 3.2 mg/dL (baseline 1.2), lactate 5.8 mmol/L, procalcitonin 48 ng/mL, platelets 82,000/mcL. Urinalysis shows too numerous to count WBC and bacteria. SOFA score is 11. Blood and urine cultures are obtained, and broad-spectrum antibiotics and IV fluid resuscitation are initiated.

A 38-year-old man is brought in by ambulance after sudden onset of severe vertigo, diplopia, and difficulty swallowing while at work 90 minutes ago. He has no significant past medical history and takes no medications. On examination, he is alert but dysarthric. Vital signs: T 37.0C, HR 78, RR 16, BP 168/94, SpO2 98%. Neurological exam reveals left-sided Horner syndrome, right-sided limb ataxia, decreased pain and temperature sensation on the left face and right body, and absent gag reflex on the left. CT head is negative for hemorrhage. CT angiography reveals left vertebral artery occlusion. NIHSS score is 12.

A 68-year-old man with a recent diagnosis of mild heart failure comes to the office because of a
1-week history of dyspnea on exertion. He is relatively sedentary but is usually able to climb a
flight of stairs without stopping. Now he must stop every few steps to rest because of dyspnea
but not chest discomfort. He also complains of lower extremity edema, 2-pillow orthopnea,
cough with occasional production of white phlegm, wheezing, and a 3-kg weight gain. He denies
chest pain or discomfort, palpitations, syncope or near syncope. He has had no fever or upper
respiratory symptoms. He states he has been compliant with his medications and denies any
changes to his diet. He was seen by another physician two times in the past few months for
similar symptoms; both times he had an ECG and chest x-ray and was told he had "mild heart
failure." He was treated with an increased dose of furosemide without any other workup.

A 50-year-old obese man with a BMI of 34 presents with a 6-month history of persistent heartburn and acid regurgitation despite taking omeprazole 20 mg daily. He reports the heartburn is worse after large meals and when lying down, and he frequently wakes at night with a sour taste in his mouth and occasional coughing. He has tried elevating the head of his bed and avoiding late meals with only partial relief. He denies dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, or hematemesis. He drinks two to three beers on weekends and does not smoke. On examination, vital signs are normal. He is an obese man in no acute distress. Abdominal exam reveals mild epigastric tenderness. There is no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. His dentist has noted enamel erosion on posterior teeth.

A 28-year-old woman presents with pain on the index finger of her left hand after accidentally touching a hot pan while cooking approximately 1 hour ago. She ran the finger under cool water immediately. She denies blistering, numbness, or limited range of motion. On examination, there is diffuse erythema of the palmar surface of the left index finger from the fingertip to the proximal interphalangeal joint. The skin is intact with no blistering or blanching. The area is tender to light touch and warm. Capillary refill is less than 2 seconds. Sensation and range of motion of the finger are intact.

A 20-year-old female college student presents with bilateral itchy, watery eyes for the past 3 days. She reports that the symptoms began shortly after spring pollen counts increased. She has a known history of seasonal allergies but has not yet started any medications this year. She denies eye pain, photophobia, purulent discharge, or changes in vision. On examination, bilateral conjunctival injection is noted with mild chemosis. There is clear watery discharge. Pupils are equal and reactive. Visual acuity is intact bilaterally. There is no preauricular lymphadenopathy.

A 26-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 3-day history of lower abdominal pain. She is 18 weeks pregnant by dates. The patient describes the pain as sharp, steady, and radiating across her lower abdomen bilaterally. Last night she developed new nausea and vomiting. She has not been able to keep down any food or drink this morning. She had a normal bowel movement yesterday. She says she felt cold and shivering this morning, followed by feeling warm; however, she did not check her temperature. She denies vaginal bleeding.

A 10-year-old girl is brought in by her parents who report she frequently feels nauseated and dizzy during car rides, particularly on winding roads. Symptoms have been occurring for the past year and typically resolve within 15 to 20 minutes after stopping the vehicle. She does not vomit. Sitting in the front seat and looking out the window helps somewhat. She denies hearing loss, tinnitus, headaches, or similar symptoms outside of car rides. On examination, she is well-appearing and in no distress. Vital signs are age-appropriate. Neurological exam, including cranial nerves and cerebellar testing, is normal. Otoscopic exam is unremarkable.

A 50-year-old man presents with intermittent burning sensation in the substernal area that he has experienced occasionally over the past several weeks. The burning typically occurs 30 to 60 minutes after large meals, particularly those that are spicy or high in fat. The discomfort is relieved within minutes by over-the-counter antacids. He denies dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, hematemesis, or melena. He has no cardiac history. On examination, vital signs are normal. The abdomen is soft, non-tender, and non-distended. There is no epigastric tenderness. Cardiac exam is unremarkable.

A 60-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of progressively worsening left lower quadrant abdominal pain that is constant and dull. She reports low-grade fever and mild nausea but no vomiting. She had a colonoscopy 2 years ago that showed extensive diverticulosis of the sigmoid colon. Her diet is low in fiber. She reports one episode of constipation followed by loose stools. Vital signs show temperature 100.8°F, heart rate 86, blood pressure 128/76. On examination, there is moderate tenderness in the left lower quadrant with voluntary guarding but no rebound tenderness or rigidity. Bowel sounds are present and hypoactive. There is no palpable mass. Laboratory work shows a white blood cell count of 13,200 with a left shift. CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast demonstrates sigmoid diverticulitis with pericolic fat stranding and no abscess or perforation.

A 12-year-old boy is brought to the office by his mother for a well-child checkup. The patient and his mother both state that the patient has been otherwise well except for occasional mild pain and stiffness in the upper back. Symptoms began gradually about a year ago and are present intermittently. The pain and stiffness do not bother him significantly or limit his activities, and they have never awakened him from sleep. He denies any trauma or overuse. He is not currently playing any organized sports although he is able to be normally active with friends and siblings.

A 19-year-old female college student is brought in by her roommate with a 24-hour history of high fever, diffuse rash, vomiting, profuse watery diarrhea, and progressive lightheadedness. She reports using a menstrual tampon that she forgot to change for approximately 3 days. On examination, she appears acutely ill with a diffuse, blanching, erythematous macular rash resembling a sunburn covering the trunk and extremities, including the palms and soles. Vital signs: T 40.2C, HR 136, RR 26, BP 72/40, SpO2 94%. Mucous membranes are hyperemic. Pelvic exam reveals a retained tampon, which is removed, and there is no evidence of abscess. Labs: WBC 15,400/mcL, platelets 88,000/mcL, creatinine 2.8 mg/dL, AST 245 U/L, ALT 198 U/L, CK 1,240 U/L. Blood cultures are drawn and empiric clindamycin and vancomycin are initiated.

A 32-year-old male singer presents with a hoarse voice that has persisted for 3 days following an intense concert performance. He reports mild sore throat and throat dryness but denies dyspnea, stridor, dysphagia, fever, or hemoptysis. He is a non-smoker and does not consume alcohol regularly. He has no history of GERD or thyroid disease. On examination, he is afebrile. The oropharynx is mildly erythematous without exudates or lesions. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy. His voice is notably hoarse and breathy. Respiratory effort is normal with no stridor or wheezing on auscultation.

A 6-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents after 8 hours of progressive wheezing and respiratory distress despite using his albuterol inhaler every 20 minutes at home. He has a history of moderate persistent asthma with two prior ICU admissions. He recently had an upper respiratory infection. On examination, he is sitting upright, using accessory muscles, and speaking in single words only. Vital signs: T 37.8C, HR 152, RR 42, BP 100/65, SpO2 87% on room air. Lung auscultation reveals markedly diminished breath sounds bilaterally with minimal wheezing, suggesting severe air trapping. Peak flow is unobtainable due to patient fatigue. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.28, pCO2 55 mmHg.

A 53-yr-old woman comes to the office because of palpitations. She is a current patient there
and has a history of well-controlled hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and tension headaches. She
states that she has noticed intermittent palpitations over the past 2 mo. She describes the
episodes as a sensation of irregular and racing heartbeats that are accompanied by fatigue.
She denies any chest pain, shortness of breath, light-headedness, or syncope. The episodes
last from 10 min to several hours, occur once or twice/wk, and resolve on their own. The last
episode was 3 days ago. She cannot identify any particular triggers. She is generally active and
walks 3 miles several days/wk without any exertional symptoms including chest pain and
dyspnea. She has no family history of early cardiac disease or sudden death. She denies any
recent fever or infectious symptoms.

A 72-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history and known COPD (GOLD stage II) presents with a 5-day history of increased sputum production and mild worsening of his baseline dyspnea. He reports his sputum has changed from white to yellow-green. He denies fever, chest pain, hemoptysis, or significant increase in cough frequency. He is currently using tiotropium and an albuterol rescue inhaler as needed. Vital signs show temperature 98.6°F, heart rate 82, blood pressure 134/78, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 93% on room air (baseline 94-95%). On examination, there is mild bilateral expiratory wheezing without accessory muscle use. He is speaking in full sentences comfortably.

A 72-year-old woman presents with generalized dry, itchy skin that has been worsening over the past several weeks as winter has progressed. She reports the itching is worst on her shins and forearms. She bathes daily in hot water and uses regular bar soap. She denies any new medications, rash, jaundice, or unintentional weight loss. On examination, the skin on the extremities is diffusely dry with fine scaling and superficial cracking. There are no excoriations, erythematous plaques, or papules. Skin turgor is appropriate for age. No jaundice or lymphadenopathy is noted.

A 20-year-old female college student who recently started a running program presents with bilateral dull, aching pain along the front of both shins. The pain began about 1 week ago and occurs primarily during and shortly after running, then resolves with rest. She runs on paved surfaces in her current athletic shoes that are over a year old. She denies pain at rest, nighttime pain, swelling, or history of stress fractures. On examination, there is mild tenderness on palpation along the medial border of the bilateral tibias spanning approximately 5 cm. There is no point tenderness, edema, or erythema. Ankle range of motion and strength are normal.

A 17-year-old female is brought in by her parents after they discovered an empty bottle of extra-strength acetaminophen (500 mg tablets, 50-count) in her room. She admits to intentionally ingesting approximately 25 grams 12 hours ago following a breakup. She initially felt fine but now reports nausea, vomiting, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. On examination, she is tearful but cooperative. Vital signs: T 37.2C, HR 96, RR 18, BP 112/68, SpO2 99%. Abdomen is tender in the right upper quadrant. Scleral icterus is not yet present. Labs: acetaminophen level 180 mcg/mL (well above treatment line on Rumack-Matthew nomogram at 12 hours), AST 1,240 U/L, ALT 1,086 U/L, INR 1.8, total bilirubin 2.1 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, pH 7.34, lactate 2.8 mmol/L. N-acetylcysteine infusion is initiated immediately. Psychiatry and social work consultations are placed. Poison control is contacted.

A 70-year-old man presents with 18 hours of worsening right upper quadrant pain, fever with rigors, and progressive yellowing of his skin and eyes. He has a history of choledocholithiasis with a prior ERCP and sphincterotomy 5 years ago. On examination, he appears jaundiced and acutely ill with intermittent rigors. Vital signs: T 39.6C, HR 118, RR 22, BP 88/52, SpO2 96%. Abdominal examination reveals significant right upper quadrant tenderness with a positive Murphy sign. Scleral icterus is prominent. Labs: WBC 22,600/mcL with 15% bands, total bilirubin 8.4 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 6.8 mg/dL, ALP 482 U/L, AST 188 U/L, ALT 162 U/L, lipase normal, lactate 4.1 mmol/L. Blood cultures are drawn. Right upper quadrant ultrasound shows common bile duct dilation to 14 mm with a shadowing stone in the distal CBD and mild intrahepatic ductal dilation.

A 3-year-old girl is brought in by her mother with a low-grade fever of 37.8°C and small blisters noticed on her hands and feet since this morning. The mother also notes a few small sores inside the child's mouth. The child is eating and drinking well, though slightly fussier than usual. Several children at her daycare have had similar symptoms. On examination, there are scattered small vesicles on the palms, soles, and a few on the dorsal hands. Two shallow ulcers are seen on the buccal mucosa. The child is alert, playful, and well-hydrated.

A 68-yr-old woman comes to the office with her daughter because of a 4-mo history of gradually
increasing lethargy and worsening memory. Her daughter is concerned because the mother has
stopped remembering whether she has taken her regular medications. The daughter is worried
that her mother might not be safe to live on her own. Prior to 4 mo ago, the woman had been
very busy with community activities, which she has since stopped, and her daughter had not
noticed any memory difficulties. The daughter is not aware of any recent illnesses or injuries.

Mrs. L is a 61 year-old woman who presents with 4 days of a cough productive of yellow sputum. Her symptoms started 4 days ago with rhinorrhea and productive cough. She initially had fevers as high as 101 for 2 days, but those have now resolved. In the office, she has normal vital signs and a normal physical examination. She is otherwise healthy except for high cholesterol for which she is being treated with atorvastatin. She has no drug allergies.

A 9-month-old male infant is brought in by his parents after 8 hours of episodic inconsolable crying during which he draws his legs up to his abdomen, alternating with periods of lethargy. The parents report two episodes of vomiting and one bowel movement containing dark red mucus-like material. He had a viral upper respiratory infection last week. On examination, during a pain-free interval, the infant is pale and lethargic. Vital signs: T 37.4C, HR 168, RR 36, BP 80/52. Abdomen is mildly distended with a palpable sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant. The right lower quadrant feels empty (Dance sign). Rectal exam reveals currant jelly stool on the examining finger. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates a target sign (doughnut sign) in the right upper quadrant, confirming ileocolic intussusception, with no evidence of perforation or peritonitis. Air enema reduction is arranged.

A 70-year-old man with a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia presents to his primary care physician with a 3-day history of dysuria, urinary frequency, and urgency. He reports mild suprapubic discomfort and low-grade fever of 100.4°F. He denies flank pain, rigors, or hematuria. His past medical history is notable for BPH managed with tamsulosin. On examination, he appears mildly uncomfortable but is in no acute distress. Vital signs show temperature 100.4°F, blood pressure 138/82, heart rate 78. Abdominal examination reveals mild suprapubic tenderness without guarding. Digital rectal exam shows an enlarged, nontender prostate. Urinalysis demonstrates pyuria and positive nitrites.

A 66-year-old woman presents with 2 days of progressive abdominal distension, diffuse crampy abdominal pain, and intractable vomiting that has become bilious and feculent. She has not passed flatus or had a bowel movement for 36 hours. Her surgical history includes an open appendectomy 30 years ago and a total abdominal hysterectomy 15 years ago. On examination, she appears dehydrated and in moderate distress. Vital signs: T 37.8C, HR 110, RR 20, BP 108/68, SpO2 97%. Abdomen is markedly distended and tympanitic with high-pitched tinkling bowel sounds. There is diffuse tenderness, greatest in the periumbilical region, with mild involuntary guarding. Labs: WBC 14,800/mcL, BUN 42, creatinine 1.6, lactate 3.1 mmol/L. CT abdomen demonstrates dilated small bowel loops up to 5.2 cm with a discrete transition point in the right lower quadrant with a small bowel feces sign and possible closed-loop configuration.

A 40-year-old male construction worker is extricated by rescue crews after being trapped under a collapsed concrete wall at a building site for approximately 4 hours. Both lower extremities were pinned. Upon extrication, he is alert and reports severe pain in both legs and a sensation of numbness. He has no significant past medical history. On examination, both lower extremities are markedly swollen, tense, and ecchymotic from the thighs to the ankles. Vital signs: T 36.4C, HR 118, RR 24, BP 96/62, SpO2 95%. Pedal pulses are weak bilaterally. Sensation is diminished throughout both legs. He reports dark brown urine since a Foley catheter was placed in the field, with only 50 mL output over the past 2 hours. Labs drawn immediately: potassium 6.8 mEq/L, creatinine 3.4 mg/dL, CK 124,000 U/L, phosphorus 7.6 mg/dL, calcium 6.2 mg/dL, uric acid 14.2 mg/dL, myoglobin 48,000 ng/mL, bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, lactate 6.8 mmol/L. ECG shows peaked T waves. Aggressive IV normal saline resuscitation at 1.5 L/hr with sodium bicarbonate supplementation is initiated, along with continuous cardiac monitoring and IV calcium gluconate for cardioprotection.

A 47-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of the worst headache of her life that began 1 hour ago while straining during a bowel movement. She describes it as a thunderclap headache reaching maximum intensity within seconds. She experienced one episode of vomiting and brief loss of consciousness. Her past medical history includes migraines and she is a current smoker. On examination, she is photophobic, irritable, and has a stiff neck. Vital signs: T 37.4C, HR 96, RR 18, BP 178/96, SpO2 98%. Neurological exam reveals intact cranial nerves, mild bilateral lower extremity weakness, and pronounced nuchal rigidity. Hunt and Hess grade III. Non-contrast CT head reveals diffuse subarachnoid hemorrhage in the basal cisterns. CT angiography identifies a 7 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm.

A 5-month-old baby boy presents with difficulty and delay in passing hard stools. His mother reports that he strains for several hours and may even miss a day, before passing stool with screaming and occasional spots of fresh blood on the stool or diaper. He has recently been weaned from breastfeeding to cows' milk formula, which he had been reluctant to drink initially. The child is thriving and now feeding normally. There was no neonatal delay in defecation and no history of excessive vomiting or abdominal distension.

A 65-year-old man presents to the emergency department with acute onset of SOB of 30 minutes' duration. Initially, he felt faint but did not lose consciousness. He is complaining of left-sided chest pain that worsens on deep inspiration. He has no history of cardiopulmonary disease. A week ago he underwent a total left hip replacement and, following discharge, was on bed rest for 3 days due to poorly controlled pain. He subsequently noticed swelling in his left calf, which is tender on examination. His current vital signs reveal a fever of 100.4°F (38.0°C), heart rate 112 bpm, BP 95/65, and an O2 saturation on room air of 91%.

A 32-year-old woman at 34 weeks gestation (G3P2) presents with sudden onset of painful vaginal bleeding and severe constant abdominal pain that began 30 minutes ago. She has a history of chronic hypertension managed with labetalol and a prior placental abruption with her second pregnancy. She reports the baby's movements have decreased since the bleeding started. On examination, she is anxious, pale, and in significant distress. Vital signs: T 36.8C, HR 124, RR 24, BP 96/62, SpO2 96%. The uterus is firm, tender, and contracted (woody consistency) with no relaxation between contractions. Moderate dark red vaginal bleeding is present.
